entries.title: ‘It’s like the wild west’: how AI has rocked the literary world
entries.summary: With authors losing lucrative deals and writers removed from prize shortlists, accusations of AI use are sending shock waves through the publishing industry. Is it too late to turn the tide on machine writing?The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn
entries.content:
The romance novelist Coral Hart got her break writing books for Mills & Boon, the publisher of bodice-ripper paperbacks. In 2012, she decided to dip her toe in self-publishing. She felt drawn to dark romance, a subgenre featuring twisted, toxic love stories that was taking off online but that publishers didn’t want to touch. Three years later, things were going well enough that she decided to self-publish full-time.

Kindle Unlimited, where Hart sells her books, rewards prolific writers: the algorithm favours those who can produce a new book at least once a month. Hart says she knows of authors who hire more than a dozen ghostwriters to keep pace. By herself, Hart can write 10,000 words a day, but AI could help her produce many more. Since 2025 she has written 370 novels under 21 pen names using AI, earning herself “high six figures”.

Like any Kindle Unlimited author, she is only paid per pages read: it would make no business sense for her to churn out books that readers quickly abandon. “A bad writer or a bad storyteller is not going to get a good book out of AI. You still need to understand craft. You still need to understand structure. You still need to know what a reader wants,” she tells me, speaking via videocall from her home in South Africa. “So, it’s not taking the human out of the equation. It’s taking the friction and the time and the business blocks out of the way.”

One study (awaiting peer review), led by Tuhin Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University, estimates that around one fifth of recently self-published books contain at least 25% AI-generated text. Hart now teaches courses on how to use AI to produce books. Unless disclosing the use of AI becomes a legal requirement, she advises other authors not to do so because of the public response.

“The minute someone discloses [AI use] they get death threats, they get called names, they’re ousted,” she says. Hart is one of her pen names. After she talked to the New York Times earlier this year she was doxed and faced death threats. “I think the anger and hate comes from a place of fear,” she says. In the literary world, many people fear the tech will undercut and replace them. “I think people are very afraid of AI, and people in publishing are delusional in thinking that it’s not going to overtake our industry, that their screaming on social media is going to stop it.”

But the anger comes from another place, too. If large language models can spit out books that people want to read, or produce a convincing pastiche of your favourite writer, that’s almost certainly because they were trained on established writers’ stolen work. Last year, a class action lawsuit involving around 500,000 titles won a $1.5bn settlement from the AI firm Anthropic for alleged use of the writers’ work without consent. Other similar lawsuits are ongoing. Many writers oppose AI for both moral and aesthetic reasons. One group of 70 prominent authors wrote an open letter calling on the big five publishers – Penguin Random House, Hachette, HarperCollins, Simon & Schuster and Macmillan – to promise that they will “never release books that were created by a machine”. The publishers did not promise.

So where do we go from here? Will big name writers win the argument for keeping AI out of literature, or will our bookshelves and e-readers soon be crammed full of AI-generated stories? And if a reader can’t distinguish human from machine writing, does it still matter?

One literary agent told me that when it comes to AI, the atmosphere in mainstream publishing is like “the wild west”. The technology is outpacing the industry’s capacity to reckon with what it means that authors can – and already are – using AI to write their books. “We’re at a time where it’s all very much in flux, and I don’t think anyone has good answers – but certainly everyone’s talking about it,” says Liz Gately, a New York-based book scout.

Instead, there has been a spate of cancelled high-profile book deals and accusations against writers. In March, Hachette withdrew the romance novel Shy Girl from publication over evidence the author Mia Ballard used AI. Ballard claimed to the New York Times that an editor she hired may have been responsible for inserting AI-generated text. This year’s winner of the Commonwealth short story prize, Jamir Nazir, was accused of using AI, after readers – struck by odd phrases such as “she had the kind of walking that turned benches into men” – ran the story through Pangram, a leading AI detection program. He denies it. Pangram subsequently tested other entrants and concluded that since 2025, four regional winners were likely to have used AI.

In July, agents representing the debut novelist Jerry Falade withdrew from an eye-popping $2m (£1.5m) book deal after he was accused of using AI. He denied using AI for anything other than research. And then, last month, the Canadian-Haitian author Thélyson Orélien’s novel was struck off the Goncourt Academy longlist, France’s most prestigious literary prize, after social media users ran his novel through AI detection software. He, too, denied using AI to write his novel, but did admit to plagiarism in some of his other writing, including a short story he wrote more than a decade ago. After conducting its own investigation, his publishers Boréal dropped him in late October.

Falade – who like everyone I contacted in relation to these scandals declined to speak to me on record – wrote an essay pointing out that writing by non-native speakers or in “culturally unfamiliar” English is more often treated with suspicion. He also suggests the accusations against him may be tinged with racism. “I haven’t seen this kind of investigative zeal directed at white authors accused of using AI …” he writes, “apparently that level of scrutiny is reserved for a Black boy from Nigeria.”

It is true that every writer at the centre of these AI scandals has been an author of colour. In May, the author Steven Rosenbaum – who is white – was found to have accidentally inserted fabricated quotes into his book The Future of Truth: How AI Reshapes Reality when he used AI, which he disclosed in the acknowledgements. He said he regretted the errors but added that it “serves as a warning about the risks of AI-assisted research and verification”, which is why he wrote the book. His book wasn’t withdrawn.

One big problem is that when writers are accused, it is hard for them to clear their names. There is no definitive proof either way. Literary agents and book scouts are professional readers and say most AI-generated submissions (and these days they receive many) are very easy to spot. But, clearly, human judgment isn’t flawless, and evidence suggests that non-native and neurodivergent writers are more likely to raise false suspicion. Academic research estimates that Pangram is at least 95% accurate at detecting AI-generated writing, and it has near-0% rate of false positives – suggesting it is extremely unlikely that the tech would falsely label human-generated writing as AI.

Hannah Bowman, chair of the Association of American Literary Agents’ (AALA) AI special committee, says there’s disagreement on the way forward: some agents think AI detection software should be used routinely, others advocate for relying on relationships of trust. “I think it’s a shame that all of these things are getting addressed so publicly,” she says, with many scandals starting when journalists or social media users run work through AI detectors. “I worry for authors when they don’t have a chance to make a case in defence of their work … there needs to be a fair and thoughtful process, where if publishers and agents have concerns, they can discuss them with the authors.”

In the meantime, Gately, the book scout, says many agents have started recommending their writers don’t send documents as PDFs and save multiple drafts of their work (rather than resaving the same document) in case they are subject to AI accusations. The pervasive anxiety among agents and writers manifests in strange ways. One agent told me they were shocked to receive a manuscript from a writer they had worked with for many years – and who professed to hate AI – that used suspiciously “bizarre” words. She contacted the writer, who was “horrified”: the problem wasn’t that she’d used AI; it was that she was terrified of being accused of doing so and her efforts to make her prose sound “non-AI” had backfired badly.

Another unresolved question is if and when publishers should withdraw books. If Falade’s book was good enough to impress multiple publishers and attract an astonishingly high, multimillion-dollar advance, does it matter how it was written? (Falade, incidentally, has recently signed with a new agent.)

Thad McIllroy, a publishing expert and author of The AI Book Revolution, says he was surprised when Shy Girl was cancelled. The cancellation was partly his fault. After being alerted to online rumours that the book was written using AI, he decided to run it through Pangram, and then approached the New York Times. “I felt so stupid when [Hachette] cancelled it because it never occurred to me that that would have been the response,” he tells me. He anticipated that the publishers would either clean up the text or issue a disclosure on how AI was used. Shy Girl started out as a highly successful self-published novel, and the AI rumours started before Hachette acquired the manuscript. Once bought, the publishers edited the text considerably. McIllroy says he therefore finds it hard to believe that no one raised AI-concerns internally. Plus, he says, it’s a “really powerful book” that clearly resonated with readers, so why drop it the moment the story hit the media?

Both AI enthusiasts and haters say there’s an urgent need for more guidance from publishers, who hold the purse strings and are therefore the kingmakers in the books’ world. McIllroy says publishers need to be “brave” and publish extensive AI policies, outlining how they use the technology in-house and what authors are and aren’t allowed to do. He wonders if publishing houses aren’t doing this because they are in denial about AI, or if they are worried about alienating their highest-earning writers, who are almost all vehemently opposed to the tech. Tess Callero, a literary agent with Europa Content who describes the prospect of AI-generated fiction as “scary”, says she thinks publishers are biding their time because they want to keep the door open for AI. “If the big five publishers were coming down and saying we will not accept [AI-generated writing] it would be taken more seriously,” she says. “But they’re not, and you have to wonder the reason they aren’t. Is it because they see a future in which potentially these books could be monetised?”

One issue is US copyright law, which specifies that a book must be “human authored” and considers AI-generated text public domain. “Which is why it’s so problematic for publishers – because if it’s AI, they have no protection, they can’t have exclusive rights,” says Natalie Lakosil, a literary agent and chair of the copyright committee at the AALA. US copyright law protects AI-assisted work, but if the text has been produced by a machine it risks legal challenge (even if the copyright office, which asks for little detail, accepts the registration). It seems likely, Lakosil says, that this principle will be challenged in the courts eventually, but she is doubtful that the “human authored” requirement will be substantially changed. “The purpose of copyright protection is to protect human creation, to protect artists, and AI is not an artist,” she says. That said, she does believe the law needs to find ways to accommodate writers who want to experiment creatively with AI. She says publishing is in the midst of a “freakout period” comparable to the advent of e-books, which didn’t kill the market – as many feared – but did permanently change it.

In 2023, Stephen Marche wrote the crime novella, Death of an Author, using three AI programs – it is, to anyone’s knowledge, the first AI-novel to be reviewed by the New York Times. It could only be released as an audiobook, because of copyright concerns. Marche has been experimenting with AI in his fiction since the early 2020s. “Publishing has both become incredibly moralistic and at the same time it keeps getting rocked by these scandals,” he tells me. “The people like me who are very conscious about its use, and who both understand the technology and its limits and are not using it in a cheap way, in a cheating way, we’re totally excluded. But you know the scammers will find a way.” He says he would love to see an “experimental blossoming of creative forms” using AI, as is already happening in the art world.

The way forward, Marche says, is full transparency: there is a “very clear moral line” in labelling what is and isn’t AI generated, just as we currently distinguish between fiction and nonfiction. Even those who hate the idea of AI writing (myself included) might recognise that on rare occasions it can be powerful, precisely when it is not trying to pass as human. In Vauhini Vara’s moving essay Ghosts, for example, she uses generative AI to express things she cannot bring herself to write about her sister’s death. The piece is a conversation between a human and a machine that explores the expressive limits, and possibilities, of both kinds of language.

Most likely, AI-generated books will enter mainstream publishing in some form, and will introduce more slop into the market. But Marche points out that our culture is already awash with dull, derivative stuff. He recently went to see a Hollywood action movie that was so formulaic that although it was not made with AI it may as well have been. “There’s this garbage out there that’s worthless, some of it is AI generated, some of it’s human generated. You’re trying to make meaningful shit in this context and how do you do that? Some of it’s going to be made by people. Some of it with AI,” he says.

In France, a new prize – the Prix Pascal de Littérature IA – was launched last month for fiction writers who are working with AI. It seems probable that some AI-assisted books will be good enough that discerning readers cannot necessarily tell that a human has not written them. A recent study, also led by Chakrabarty of Stony Brook University and awaiting peer review, found that in blind experiments, when expert readers (students on leading MFA writing programmes) compared passages written by their MFA colleagues and those written by AI models trained on established writers, and then fine-tuned, they tended to prefer the AI generated text. Would they still prefer the texts if they knew they were AI? Maybe some people will be happy to read such books, although even the most beautiful AI-generated text is a Frankenstein monster, borrowed feelings and observations about the human condition stitched together by an algorithm that has no human qualities, no capacity to love or to feel. But probably many readers would choose human writing. Every agent I spoke to felt committed to protecting the human. “We’re in the human creativity business, not in the business of giving robots jobs,” says Doug Wallace, managing director at Andrew Nurnberg Associates International, a network of literary agencies. AI is “not going to be a big problem because we won’t let it become a big problem”.

But then again, as a writer of course I would want to conclude there. Right now, to write without the aid of a machine is to swim against a strong cultural tide. I’ve lost track of how many friends, in professions other than journalism, have looked at me with something close to pity when I tell them I would never use AI to write, not only because of my contractual obligations or the reputational risk but because I still think I can offer something better than a machine. And yet, machine-generated language keeps cropping up in the places you’d expect to offer the greatest resistance to slop: not just in book submissions but in leading newspapers and literary magazines. Among the many minor AI news stories to bubble up while I worked on this article? A piece in the Times Literary Supplement on AI and the crisis of the author, which was removed from the website because of – you guessed it – allegations it had been written with AI.

entries.title: The best books to read in November and December: new paperbacks from Benjamin Myers, Jeanette Winterson and John Updike
entries.summary: Looking for a new reading recommendation? Here are some must-read new paperbacks, from an experimental novel about a German actor to a study of how the arts can boost our health*** Continue reading...
entries.content:
Fiction

Fiction

Jesus Christ Kinski

Benjamin Myers

The German actor Klaus Kinski is known best for his testy collaboration with Werner Herzog, whose 1982 film Fitzcarraldo put Kinski in the title role, lugging a steamship over the Andes.

Benjamin Myers’s new novel plunges us into Kinski’s fevered mind during one of his last performances, a recorded solo stage show in West Berlin in 1971, where he delivered a ferocious monologue as Jesus. Showcased in a documentary released in 2008 by Peter Geyer, the act descended into chaos, Kinski arguing with hecklers before ending his monologue in a near-empty auditorium.

The book melds Kinski’s on-the-record words with imagined second-person recollection about, among other things, his capture by allied forces as a German conscript, a spell in a psychiatric clinic, and his innumerable sexual conquests.

Cut half a century later to West Yorkshire during lockdown, where an unnamed writer decides to write a book “about the dead German actor Klaus Kinski”. The project looks unsaleable from the off, not least because Kinski’s eldest daughter, Pola, accused him of sexually abusing her. There’s also the fact that “the writer” – let’s call him Benjamin Myers – owes his publisher a “long, era-spanning historical novel concerning an English saint”, and has already spent the advance (this is a reference to 2023’s Goldsmiths prize-winning Cuddy). Yet the “dark and forceful energy” of Kinski’s Jesus keeps drawing him back to online footage. By the time Myers clocks that the actor was 45 in 1971 – the age Myers is in 2021 – “a psychic door of communication [is] opened by the key of coincidence”, and it would basically be rude not to write the book.

This fitfully engaging narrative experiment isn’t really about Kinski or even Myers so much as the 21st-century cultural marketplace. As lapel-grabbing rants give way to downbeat musings, the book exerts a strange charm, ushering us behind the scenes of its own making. “I live freely,” Kinski boasts, unlike people “stuck in … dismal jobs”. Amid the keynote disaffection, you ultimately sense contentment, even joy, that he’s not the only one able to say so. Anthony Cummins

£8.99 (RRP £9.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Fiction

The True True Story of Raja the Gullible (and His Mother)

Rabih Alameddine

Meet Raja, the narrator of Rabih Alameddine’s new novel. A 63-year-old gay philosophy teacher and drag entertainer, he is a stickler for rules and boundaries, living in a tiny Beirut flat with his octogenarian mother, the nosy and unfettered Zalfa. Invited to a writing residency in the US, Raja will use the occasion to relate his life.

Winner of the 2025 US National Book Award for fiction, Alameddine’s seventh novel opens and closes in 2023, but the bulk of its action takes place earlier: encompassing the lead-up to and aftermath of the Lebanese civil war (1975-1990), the Covid pandemic, Lebanon’s 2019 banking crisis, and the Beirut port explosion in 2020. If this timeline makes the book sound like a punishing tour of Lebanese history, I promise it isn’t. More than a war chronicle or national exposé, it is a queer coming-of-age tale, an exploration of the bond between a mother and a son, and a meditation on storytelling, memory, survival and what it means to be truly free. Told in a voice as irresistibly buoyant as it is unapologetically camp, this rule-breaking spin on the trauma plot holds on to its cheer in the face of sobering material. Poignant but never cynical, often dark but never dour, wise without being showy and always eager to crack a joke, this is a novel that insists that the pain of the past need overwhelm neither present nor narrative, identity nor personality. With Sartre as his guide, and a drag fabulousness all his own, Raja shows us how. Yagnishsing Dawoor

£9.89 (RRP £10.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Crime and thriller

Crime and thriller

A Bad, Bad Place

Frances Crawford

Set in the late 1970s in the Possilpark district of Glasgow, an area riven by poverty, crime and sectarianism, Crawford’s superb debut is told from two points of view: 12-year-old Janey, who is walking her dog when she stumbles upon the body of a young woman; and her grandmother Maggie, who has cared for Janey since she was rescued, as a baby, from the gas explosion that killed her immediate family. Janey is afraid to tell the police all she knows, but finds herself caught up in the machinations of the grownup world. Maggie, who has secrets of her own, is desperate to protect her granddaughter, but poverty and lack of choice make her vulnerable, and the dead woman has connections to a well-known criminal family. A well-observed, well-told account of trauma, grief and the concomitant magical thinking, this coming-of-age mystery has flashes of humour and pathos that provide fuel for real suspense. Laura Wilson

£8.99 – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Crime and thriller

The Madman

Henning Mankell, translated by George Goulding and Sarah de Senarclens

Written in the 1970s and published in English for the first time, The Madman is set in a Swedish town in the late 1940s. The country’s wartime neutrality-on-paper continues to divide: the town’s pro-Nazis want the past forgotten, but the communist sympathisers, bitter about having been interned, want a reckoning. When a letter to this effect appears in the local paper, those accused, including the director of the town’s sawmill, claim that newcomer Bertil Kras has been stirring resentment for political ends. When the sawmill burns down, Kras is blamed for that, too, and the disintegration of the life he has tried to make provokes an existential crisis. An older Mankell might have been more concise, but the slow build towards inevitable disaster makes for true emotional depth, and the theme of othering, isolating and penalising people for their opinions remains horribly topical. Laura Wilson

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Letters

Letters

John Updike: A Life in Letters



John Updike had the mind of a middling middle-class postwar American male, and the prose style of a literary genius. Such a lord of language was he that even the notoriously grudging Vladimir Nabokov afforded him a meed of praise. A reviewer, musing on the disproportion between the style and content of Updike’s fiction, likened him to a lobster with one hugely overgrown claw. It was a comparison Updike was to remember – for all his bland urbanity, on display from start to finish in this mighty volume of his letters, he could be prickly, and did not take slights lightly.

At the heart of this volume we find the correspondence, from the first half of the 1970s, surrounding Updike’s separation and divorce from Mary, and his affair with and marriage to Martha – the biblical resonances of the names are almost too pat. These pages make for painful reading: Updike could be cruel – to Martha: “Mary’s body (her breasts!) would delight me still, if I could dissociate it from her pinched Unitarian soul …” – but in the main they are either pained, with Mary, or passionate, with Martha. And simultaneously, of course, he was having it off with other loves, old and new.

Are his books read now? Towards the end he made a glum self-assessment: “I have fallen to the status of an elderly duffer whose tales of suburban American sex are hopelessly yawnworthy period pieces.” Perhaps so; but he wrote such prose as to make the envious seraphim sigh. John Banville

£15.29 (RRP £16.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Science

Science

Art Cure

Daisy Fancourt

A professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London, Fancourt researches how social connections and behaviours affect our health. In Art Cure, her first book for a popular audience, she aims to make a scientific case that the arts – from playing music to theatre-going to painting – aren’t a merely aesthetic aspect of life. Instead, they are deeply entwined with our mental and physical wellbeing at every level – from the workings of our cells and molecules to cognition, memory and mood. In an era of shrinking arts funding and overstretched healthcare systems, her message is urgent. But how to compile rigorous evidence for something as holistic, indefinable – and, perhaps, resolutely unscientific – as art?

Fancourt’s answer is to dissect artistic interventions and practices into their component parts. She argues that every arts experience can be broken down into “active ingredients”; could even – if we had the processing power – be converted into binary code. Singing to sick babies becomes a mix of noise buffering, neurological stimulation, human contact and stress reduction. These ingredients trigger biological mechanisms that lead to health outcomes, she explains, and we can test, refine and prescribe them just as we might any cocktail of drugs. With this approach in mind, she surveys the evidence for medical benefits, from wellbeing to brain health, chronic pain and even how long we live.

Art Cure cannot provide answers. But it does make a compelling, compassionate case for broadening how we think about medicine – to encompass people and communities, not just physical bodies, and to recognise that creativity, identity and purpose shape our biology as much as any drug. Jo Marchant

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

History

History

Stay Alive: Berlin 1939-45

Ian Buruma

Berlin had always been a case apart. The legacy of the wild Weimar years – all that artistic and political radicalism, not to mention louche living – had continued under the Third Reich. The city remained defiantly itself and, despite the efforts of high command, mulish about being told what to do. That, at least, had been the situation in 1941.

By the time Ian Buruma’s father, a conscripted labourer from the Netherlands, arrived two years later, Berlin had begun grudgingly to toe the line. The war was going badly now, with the Russians pushing in from the east, and American and British bombs dropping from the skies. Food was scarce, Jewish citizens were being disappeared daily and Hitler and Goebbels, both frequently in the city, were getting more anxious and crueller by the day. Now whenever Berliners met each other in a food queue or a bomb shelter their most likely greeting was Bleiben sie übrig – “Stay alive”.

Nonetheless, argues Buruma, wherever you looked you could still find pockets of resistance. He isn’t referring here to well organised underground networks, but rather to ordinary men and women, not especially brave but still capable of doing the right thing. When Jews were ordered to start wearing identifying insignia, plenty of their fellow Berliners made a point of going up to them in the street and shaking hands. Young Leo Buruma, drafted in to work at a heavy engineering factory, took up with a Ukrainian girlfriend, pointedly ignoring the Nazis’ dictum that, as a “Germanic” Dutchman, he had no business consorting with an “inferior race”.

Other witnesses, such as journalists Ursula von Kardorff and Ruth Andreas-Friedrich, were careful to keep only scrappy and coded memos during the war, but subsequently reconstructed these into coherent narratives for publication. Von Kardorff could never be described as a resister, yet her memoir shows someone trying hard to remain decent in a criminal state. Her father, a successful portrait painter, had lost his teaching job thanks to his opposition to the regime, yet her mother, a textile designer, continued to kit out the homes of the Nazi grandees. Ursula herself delivers warm clothes to Jewish homes but wonders if she is merely doing it to salve her conscience. Her real anguish is reserved for her brother who is fighting for Germany on the eastern front.

None of this is morally coherent and yet, suggests Buruma in this wonderfully nuanced book, it was necessary if you wanted to stay alive, and knew yourself to be neither brave nor craven – but somewhere in the muddled in-between. Kathryn Hughes

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Memoir

The Uncool

Cameron Crowe

Crowe previously fictionalised his story in the 2000 film Almost Famous, which he wrote and directed. His lyrical and compulsively readable memoir The Uncool is bookended by the opening of a musical version, which coincides with the death of Crowe’s mother Alice whose aphorisms, including “Put some goodness in the world before it blows up”, are scattered throughout the book.

Crowe’s is a world of aftershow parties filled with characters like Freddie Sessler, a drug dealer who is rumoured to have made his fortune manufacturing pencils; late-night dressing-room jam sessions (Crowe has his guitar gently removed from his hands by a roadie called Red Dog when he attempts to join in with the Allman Brothers); eager, undamaged groupies (he knows a crew called the Flying Garter Girls whose leader Pennie Lane’s credo is “only blowjobs, and that’s it”); and, as the early 70s wear on, omnipresent cocaine use, though Crowe doesn’t partake. “I couldn’t shake the image of my teacher-mother popping up,” he says. “You’re killing brain cells!”

He shadowed Bowie at parties with Ronnie Wood and in the studio with Iggy Pop; he hung out with him day and night in houses he was renting, meaning that he was there to record the heartstopping moment when Bowie suddenly jumped to his feet mid-interview because he thought he’d seen a body fall from the sky.

The Uncool captures an extraordinarily inventive period in which rock music was stretching out in all directions, whether towards country music thanks to artists like Gram Parsons, or the conceptual in albums by the likes of Yes and the Who. Crowe was part of a burgeoning music press that, as well as recommending new bands to its readers, or conveying what rock groups had to say for themselves, would interpret, celebrate and contextualise the huge creative strides some of these musicians were making. Alex Needham

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Memoir

Joyride

Susan Orlean

Over the course of four decades, seven books and countless exquisite magazine features, especially for the New Yorker, Orlean has profiled celebrities and nobodies, followed cults and choirs, turned her eye to supermarkets and surfers. “Writers fall into two categories: there are those who have something they want to say to the world, and there are those who believe the world has something to tell them,” she observes. Orlean falls squarely into the second camp. There are two kinds of story she likes best: “hiding in plain sight” and “who knew?”.

A memoir is usually neither of these sorts of stories, but Orlean rises to the challenge of writing about her own life with grace. Joyride represents the liner notes to a career of hits. There’s the deliciously “heady, fun, surreal” experience of watching Spike Jonze’s movie Adaptation, based on her book The Orchid Thief, come to life – including being played by Meryl Streep. (Orlean’s account of flipping open Charlie Kaufman’s script for the first time to discover herself in it is laugh-out-loud funny.) A memorable Twitter thread from 2020 – the result of too much rosé on an empty stomach – that made her the “patron saint of pandemic drinking”, gets its moment, too. And harder episodes: a divorce, a cancer diagnosis, the sorrow of moving her mother into a nursing home.

Orlean sees the writing life as one of constant highwire creative reinvention – “you never build equity”, is how she puts it. Her father, who wanted to be writer but became a businessman instead, might have agreed: after she published The Orchid Thief he suggested she consider finally enrolling in law school. Thank goodness she didn’t. “I felt called, I really did, to describe ordinary life in a way that revealed its complexity and poetry – to show how rewarding it is to be open to and curious about the world, and how much joy can be found in letting yourself be surprised.” Mythili Rao

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Essays

Essays

One Aladdin Two Lamps

Jeanette Winterson

In the framing device that opens the Middle Eastern folk tales collected in One Thousand and One Nights, King Shahryar avenges his wife’s infidelity by ordering her execution and marrying a new virgin every night, having each of them beheaded by sunrise so they won’t have time to cheat. When he runs out of victims, the young Persian queen Shahrazad volunteers but stalls her own murder by telling the king one captivating tale after another – and those become the stories we’re reading.

As Jeanette Winterson puts it in her new book – a dizzying whirligig of memoir, history, philosophy, politics and self-help, loosely tied to commentary on the Nights – Shahrazad’s feat of creativity “refuses the present emergency – the contrived drama of a powerful man”. The echo of life in the Trump era is deliberate; for Winterson, the means by which Shahrazad changes her predicament holds out hope for a progressive politics currently losing ground to “radical-rightwing thuggery”. “A better story starts with a better story,” she writes. “Reason will not win the day. Without imagination nothing changes.”

Each chapter opens with a pithy retelling of one of Shahrazad’s tales, spritzed with 21st-century idiom (“The Vizier … has no manosphere where he can vent”), before giving way to wide-ranging reflections on anything and everything, from the history of eugenics, to 13th-century Mali, to the awfulness of the trouser suits “preferred by some CEO types and lots of female politicians”. As opinions on matters big and small fly past, the tone evokes by turns a party political broadcast, Radio 4’s Thought for the Day, an old friend setting the world to rights. Anthony Cummins

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Biography

Biography

The Curious Case of Mike Lynch

Katie Prescott

At least two terrible ironies surround the death of Mike Lynch. One lies in the name of his superyacht, which sank off the coast of Sicily in the early hours of 19 August 2024. He had named the boat Bayesian to honour Bayes’s theorem, a mathematical rule that helps you weigh up the probability of something given the available evidence, which served as Lynch’s guiding light over the course of a tempestuous career. The theorem was “a beautiful key to our minds”, Lynch believed. But it was entirely incapable of predicting the outcome that morning, when the yacht capsized during a storm, killing seven people, including Lynch, his 18-year-old daughter Hannah and his US lawyer, Chris Morvillo.

A second irony lies in the fact that Lynch had just come through the trial of his life, one he felt was bound to end in jail, where he thought he could die. Somehow, to everyone’s astonishment, an American jury had acquitted him and his co-defendant on all 15 counts of fraud.

To celebrate their win, Mike and his wife, Angela, decided to take the Bayesian on a series of cruises around southern Italy, inviting various supporters and associates. Lynch was no sailor, but he loved the seclusion the boat offered, and was immensely proud of its a 72-metre mast, one of the tallest in the world – a feature that some have speculated made it more vulnerable in strong winds, although the yacht’s manufacturer has defended its design. Through July and into August, it pottered around Capri and the Aeolian Islands. Then, in the middle of the month, the court victors were overtaken by a sequence of near-impossible coincidences, as Prescott sets out in pacily written detail. Charlie English

£10.79 (RRP £11.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

Politics

Politics

The Mission

Tim Weiner

Why has an organisation with huge amounts of money at its disposal, a record of recruiting the brightest and the best, and the widest of remits, failed to notch up a better record? It’s true that we may not know about many of the CIA’s successes. But we know about a lot of its failures, and some of them have marked US history ineradicably.

In The Mission, Tim Weiner, whose reporting on the CIA in the New York Times was always essential reading, and whose subsequent books on the US intelligence community have a place on the shelves of anyone interested in international affairs, provides a variety of answers to this essential question. As he showed nearly 20 years ago in Legacy of Ashes, his history of the CIA from its founding in 1947 to the end of the 20th century, the agency’s position by the end of the 90s was pretty desperate. It was starved of cash and bleeding talent. A high-flyer who had been station chief in Bucharest was revealed to be working for the Russians, handing them the names of large numbers of agents and employees. But the new US administration that came in at the start of 2001 wasn’t too worried. In March that year, Donald Rumsfeld, the defence secretary, told the joint chiefs of staff: “For the first time in decades, the country faces no strategic challenge.” Six months later came 9/11. The CIA had tried to convince the feckless George W Bush about the looming threat of Islamic ultra-fundamentalism, but no one in the administration listened. The agency was regarded as broken.

Weiner’s sources encompass several senior CIA figures from the period under discussion. These people opened up to him, and as a result the book contains many essential new details. Weiner’s account of Donald Trump’s links to Vladimir Putin in 2016 is clearly based on information from inside the agency, and it leads him to assert openly that Trump was Putin’s polezny idiot – his useful idiot. There are all sorts of other important and fascinating revelations in The Mission. No one has opened up the CIA to us like Weiner has. John Simpson

£11.69 (RRP £12.99) – purchase at the Guardian bookshop

entries.title: This Cursed Beautiful Land by Evan Gershkovich review – jailed in Putin’s Russia
entries.summary: The US reporter wrongly imprisoned for espionage writes compellingly about his ordealEvan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.Th
entries.content:
Evan Gershkovich is the Wall Street Journal reporter who, in the early phase of Putin’s war in Ukraine, was snatched up by the Russian authorities on bogus espionage charges and spent a year and a half in Russian jails (first Lefortovo and then Yekaterinburg) before being released in a prisoner exchange in 2024.

The opening section of his book about the experience is gripping and rather moving. He recounts his arrest in a sting operation, after meeting a contact who promised to supply him with information about Russia’s military-industrial preparations. Born to Russian Jewish immigrant parents in the US, Gershkovich grew up in suburban New Jersey on a diet of Soviet cartoons and “Krylov’s fables rather than Aesop’s”; he was betwixt and between. When he found his way into journalism in his early 20s – first working nights as an editorial assistant at the New York Times, then getting started properly as a reporter at the Moscow Times – he gravitated to Russia and fell in love with it.

Describing his life as a reporter, he gives a sense of how even a big city like Moscow, if you’re a foreign correspondent, is a village. As the Ukraine war started and the Kremlin tightened its restrictions on reporters, that village began to empty out. Some of Gershkovich’s Russian colleagues fled, the odd one was run in. Things got hairier. But calculating – wrongly, as it turned out – that Putin’s thugs would still hesitate before doing to a foreigner what they did cheerily to their own nationals, Gershkovich kept on reporting. Understandable, a little heroic, a little foolish.

His account of his time in prison is interesting and deftly written, but the narrative tires a bit after his arrest. Gershkovich is in a Russian prison; but at the same time he’s not of a Russian prison. He knows all along, essentially, that he’s a bargaining chip – that he’s going to be repatriated in a prisoner exchange: “I’m still a voyeur, I wrote in my journal. I have a way out.” It’s unpleasant, but he has a very low chance of being tortured, beaten, disappeared or sent to fight and die in Bakhmut (the latter being the fate of his teenage cellmate in Central prison in Yekaterinburg).

He spends a lot of time reading, takes up smoking again, watches terrible Russian TV (a highlight is Monastery Kitchen, where a portly chef dressed as an Orthodox priest inflicts horrid pre-revolutionary cuisine on his friend Oleg), misses his girlfriend, cherishes the chance to exercise and meditate; cooks ingeniously with the tools he has available; forms a touching bond with his Lefortovo cellmate; and, of course, keeps a diary because he knows he’s going to be able to write about all this later.

He describes well the strange kayfabe of his prosecution – Gershkovich is tormented by curiosity as to who, if anyone, really believes he’s a spy; he thinks, weirdly, that Putin actually might – and the foregone conclusions of an “investigation” in the Russian judicial system. Beria’s principle (“show me the man, and I’ll show you the crime”) is still the basic operating system of post-Soviet justice.

You learn much that’s fascinating and depressing about Russian prisons: the means of communication between cells; the etiquette (never shake hands with a cellmate until you’ve established they’re not in for a sex crime; always show respect by wiping your feet on the rag at the cell door); the punitive hierarchies; the way that the system’s prisoners come to feel more comfortable there than on the outside.

The problem is, slightly, that his ability to analyse the events he’s living through or report on the glubinka, or what you might call la Russie profonde is a little inhibited by the fact that he’s in jail. (At the very same time, Åsne Seierstad was reporting all over Russia for her book Never Say War, with Gershkovich’s situation something of which she was anxiously aware.) As the conflict with Ukraine unfolds, Gershkovich watches it on prison TV.

There are, of course, insights into the Russian mindset to be had from behind bars. Gershkovich is electrified by the Wagner chief Yevgeny Prigozhin’s abortive march on Moscow. But when the news of Prigozhin’s subsequent death in a plane accident flashes on the TV, his cellmate tells him he’d already heard about it that morning.

“‘Why didn’t you tell me?’ I thundered [...] Seryoga shrugged. ‘He existed and now he no longer does,’ he said. ‘I couldn’t care less.’”

This Cursed Beautiful Land: A Russian Story by Evan Gershkovich is published by William Collins (£25). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Public Access Afterworld by Jane Schoenbrun review – horror in the TV static
entries.summary: The Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma writer-director’s first novel is a wry, hugely fun journey into the dark world behind our screensPublic Access Afterworld is the first novel by Jane Schoenbrun, director of cult-hit horror film I Saw the TV Glow and the more recent Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma; movies in which screens are a permeable barrier and people are menaced by the uncanny rea
entries.content:
Public Access Afterworld is the first novel by Jane Schoenbrun, director of cult-hit horror film I Saw the TV Glow and the more recent Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma; movies in which screens are a permeable barrier and people are menaced by the uncanny realms that lurk behind them. Here the main character is Bethany Peters, a young trans woman working as a content moderator at a YouTube-like company called GlobalVill. Her job is to watch “offensive, illegal, disturbing videos that have no place on the internet” and press a red button to remove those that violate the code of conduct. One night she sees a video posted by someone with the username JulesPublicAccessAfterworld, a visibly malnourished non-binary kid who reminds Bethany of herself “before her stay in hospital, and everything that happened to her there”. The kid says to camera, “If you’re watching this, David Sawyer, this is for you,” then takes out a razor blade and draws it down their arm. Soon Bethany is off on a quest to save them, in the course of which she will learn that she herself is one of “the crooked”, people destined to vanish into Public Access Afterworld, the world behind the TV screen.

There are several other strands to the novel. A nameless patient at the Saint Thomas Youth Rehabilitation Center tells us about a fellow inmate “going by the name David Sawyer” who spends every night narrating a TV programme about a character called Bethany Peters. We meet David again as a lonely teenager glimpsing terrifying images in television static; then again as the cult leader and suspected serial killer to whom Jules and other aspiring “crooked” people dedicate their self-harm videos. We also go to Los Alamos in the final days of the Manhattan Project, where a troubled scientist’s wife has begun to suspect her husband of making something worse than nuclear bombs. In one bravura section we meet Chimotera, the mad scientist/monster of a Lon Chaney-era horror franchise, who is brought back to life in different avatars across successive reboots, and slowly comes to understand and resent his true nature. Schoenbrun ingeniously unites these strands in an ending that manages to be uplifting and nihilistic at the same time.

A standout feature of this novel is its centring of trans experience. This seems natural, given Schoenbrun’s gender identity as non-binary and transfeminine; but it also feels natural in the unfolding of the plot. We hardly need to be told how our Final Girl, Bethany, came to be such a canny survivor, or why she’s so prepared to find herself the focus of other people’s sick obsessions. The most memorable character, though, might be the cult acolyte Jules, a crooked person manqué who is both frightening and strangely moving. Abused by their parents and bullied by peers, they’ve become dependent on drugs, incapable of forming relationships, and enraged at their failure to matter to anyone. In their goth ghost makeup, they embody the archetype haunting almost every ghost narrative: the traumatised victim of society’s cruelty who has returned to exact vengeance.

Schoenbrun is an internet native, who started out writing in fan-fiction forums, and Public Access Afterworld has a casual, internetty tone, even when dealing with its darkest material. This novel fits into a contemporary school of cool, self-aware horror in books and on screen that is at once high-art and kitsch, moving seamlessly from cosmic terror to moody introspection to fan-friendly jokes. Think Widow’s Bay or Chuck Tingle’s Bury Your Gays or any of Schoenbrun’s own films. At one point, the narrator says to the monster Chimotera: “You eat vital organs when really you’re just eating your feelings.” Occasionally a character will pause to marvel at how far-fetched the plot has become. It does get a little far-fetched, and the world-building doesn’t always bear close inspection, but the knowing voice ensures the reader is always in on the joke. The informality of the tone is part of the appeal, but it can get a little sloppy. Here, for instance, is a description of the opening sequence of a TV show about werewolves and vampires warring in a dystopian United States: “The London Symphony Orchestra conducts, soundtracking our propulsive opening credit sequence whisking viewers over a CGI map of Second America.” However, even a sentence like this has a certain pace and charisma, and it gets the job done.

In the treatment of their core theme – the relationship between the attention economy and its victims – Schoenbrun is wonderfully brutal, passionate and astute. They powerfully draw out the horror of screen culture, making us feel how, in some way, the ugliest content on YouTube inhabits the same nightmare subreality as the catchphrases and laughtrack of an 80s sitcom. They also capture our perverse longing to enter that world, to leave human life and become the story: to flee to the other side of the screen. The nameless patient at the Saint Thomas Youth Rehabilitation Center says: “They don’t give people like us the Sunday night-time slot on HBO. They put us in hospitals. They send us to hell.” Public Access Afterworld shows us that hell, a locked psych ward and the primetime slot on HBO can all be the same place.

Public Access Afterworld by Jane Schoenbrun is published by Sceptre (£20). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Transcription by Ben Lerner audiobook review – a meditation on memory for the smartphone era
entries.summary: Actor Seth Numrich vividly captures the neurotic tendencies of a middle-aged man with a digital dependency, in an intense multilayered tale of family and storytellingWe meet the unnamed narrator of Transcription on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. He is going to interview his one-time mentor Thomas, a celebrated German writer and film-maker, who is 90 and who, owing to his age, probably won’t
entries.content:
We meet the unnamed narrator of Transcription on a train to Providence, Rhode Island. He is going to interview his one-time mentor Thomas, a celebrated German writer and film-maker, who is 90 and who, owing to his age, probably won’t be interviewed again. The narrator confesses to his young daughter, Eva, that he is nervous about the meeting. Those nerves are replaced by panic when he gets to his hotel and drops his iPhone into a sink of water, rendering it useless. Not only does he have no means of recording the interview, he won’t be able to FaceTime Eva at bedtime.

Ben Lerner’s novella is a thoughtful meditation on memory, storytelling and lives lived through technology. The middle-aged narrator’s anxiety over his phone falls away as he engages with the world around him and with his past. He is pleased at being “able to convert the sense of being screenless into a kind of super­sensitivity” though later, in Thomas’s house, he finds himself “glitching, craving my cellular phone on a cellular level, shamefully unresponsive to the old media that surrounded me”. For the interview, he pretends to record the conversation on his dead phone and tries to commit Thomas’s words to memory.

Actor Seth Numrich is the reader who ably negotiates the multilayered prose, the unusual narrative flourishes (such as Transcription’s breaking of the fourth wall) and teases out the neurotic tendencies of Lerner’s protagonist. In the final chapters, the narrator has an intense conversation with Thomas’s son, Max, which offers new perspectives on his father and exposes the murky line between truth and fiction.

Further listening

Ghost Stories

Siri Hustvedt, Sceptre, 11hr 58min

The What I Loved author narrates her book about the life and death of her husband, novelist Paul Auster, who died from cancer in 2024, reflecting on the nature of grief, memory, partnership and love.

Out Now

Scott Bryan, Blink, 5hr 55min

The TV commentator and critic combines memoir with sharp cultural analysis and interviews as he traces the evolution of queer identity and politics through some of TV’s most pivotal moments. Read by the author.

entries.title: Does M John Harrison’s Booker win mean science fiction is finally accepted by a ‘snobby’ literary establishment?
entries.summary: Kazuo Ishiguro, Jeff VanderMeer, Olivia Laing and other writers weigh in on the publishing world’s genre warsAs M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction,
entries.content:
As M John Harrison was announced as the Booker prize winner on Monday evening, the 81-year-old looked gobsmacked. Decades into his career, and long overlooked by the mainstream literary establishment, he had just won a prize that has never before rewarded a writer known for science fiction, with a decidedly fantastical book.

His fans, many leading authors among them, are thrilled. “For decades it was a standard – and correct – nerd whine to point out that sentence for sentence, book for book, Harrison was one of the greatest writers out there, full stop, but that ‘mainstream’ prizes never reflected that,” says China Miéville, who last week won the Goldsmiths prize with his 1,200-page speculative novel The Rouse. Back in 2002, Miéville wrote that Harrison not having won a Booker by that point proved “the bankruptcy and back-slapping generic snobbery of the literary establishment”. Now, he says: “I am so delighted, for Harrison, and for fiction.”

While some past Booker-winning authors draw heavily on SF – Margaret Atwood, Kazuo Ishiguro, Ian McEwan – Harrison is the first winner from the “bona fide SF” sphere, said Booker prize foundation chief executive Gaby Wood on Monday. The Pulitzer and the Nobel rarely take notice of SF either, though the latter has honoured Ishiguro and Doris Lessing – both of whom are considered literary writers who dabble in SF, rather than purists, and thus perhaps considered more palatable to a wider reading public.

Ishiguro says that when he emerged on to the British literary scene, he was “mystified” as to why the establishment had “fenced off SF into a ghetto”. He believes it’s done “real harm to the development of ‘literary fiction’ in the UK”, and he “personally felt liberated to go in that direction only in the early 2000s, after noticing – and envying – the brilliance of younger writers like David Mitchell and Alex Garland who were clearly inspired by SF, comics and games”. He notes, however, that his mentor and teacher Angela Carter had “no such prejudices”, often using SF elements in her work.

He points out the contrast between the patronising attitude of the mainstream literary establishment and that of cinema: “even the most highbrow of critics” venerated Fritz Lang’s Metropolis, Kubrick’s 2001: A Space Odyssey and Tarkovsky’s Solaris as “milestones of cinema history”.

Author and critic Olivia Laing agrees it’s taken the literary world “an embarrassingly long time to clock that you don’t need realism to write about how it feels to inhabit late capitalism and unravelling modernity”. Harrison has “finally got his dues” with this week’s win.

Harrison’s winning book, The End of Everything, might be called a polycrisis novel. It sees mysterious alien phenomena called iGhetti cropping up on Earth, where they increasingly warp the fabric of reality. The extraterrestrial beings may stand in for AI, climate degradation, political chaos, Brexit, runaway capitalism, or all of the above.

So while there are futuristic elements, the book very much feels like a story about now. “I gather that somebody at the award ceremony asked Harrison if he had ‘any predictions for the future’,” says the novelist Michel Faber. “That typifies the obtuseness of people who just don’t get what the best so-called ‘science fiction’ does.” The End of Everything is firmly about the present – “an elucidation of the future we’re already living in”, adds Faber.

The recognition will surely bring Harrison a host of new readers – perhaps even former SF sceptics, for whom the book will prove that the genre can be both literary and acutely politically current. NielsenIQ BookData reported that sales stood at 13,400 copies pre-win. Based on previous years, Harrison can expect to sell tens of thousands more copies in the months to come.

Harrison’s win is a “huge victory for the seriousness of genre fiction as a project”, says the novelist Julia Armfield, who cried when she heard the news. Though it is also a win for the type of fiction that “resists decoding”. Indeed, as Harrison said in an interview with the Guardian this week: “My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre.” He described the book as “SF-adjacent”.

Certain kinds of writing “make genre concerns seem beside the point,” says the critic and novelist Chris Power. Even in Harrison’s more purely SF books, he subverts the genre, “deconstructing sci-fi tropes and questioning the militarism of sci-fi”. Since he began writing in the 60s, he’s “always been queering the pitch”.

Harrison is a “writer’s writer before he is a science fiction writer”, agrees novelist Isabel Waidner. In a commercialised publishing culture “which tends to reward conventionality, including arguably arbitrary genre conventions”, Harrison writes fiction “that pushes preconceived ideas of what a novel is”. Power suggests Harrison’s work shows that genre brackets may be more useful from a marketing perspective than an aesthetic one. “A lot of the most interesting novels have always muddled these things,” he adds.

The novelist Jeff VanderMeer says he tries to avoid the “genre v literary” debate – he believes it’s “meaningless or, quite frankly, just kind of boring or not useful”. He adds: “What I do care about is when that debate, from either ‘side’, reduces complex works of fiction to caricatures. Or when it serves a gatekeeping function that reduces access to prestige or readers that has little relationship to the quality of the work.”

Reviewing Harrison’s 2023 “anti-memoir” Wish I Was Here, Power described Harrison as “the best British writer you’ve never heard of”. Three years on, the literary establishment has woken up, and Harrison is suddenly famous, his fans basking in the Booker glow. Waidner puts it like this: “His win is a win for literature, for us, and for that most endangered of things – thinking.”

entries.title: ‘We are dream-walking into a desperate situation’: the Booker prize winner on his sci-fi alien invasion wakeup call
entries.summary: He is a sci-fi titan but M John Harrison has just exploded into the mainstream – with The End of Everything, an apocalyptic novel set on the Kent coast. Does he really think we have no hope left?With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Bo
entries.content:
With his twinkling eyes and silver ponytail, M John Harrison doesn’t seem anything like his 81 years. The M stands for Michael, Mike to his friends. And last night he became the oldest author to win the Booker prize for fiction, for his 13th novel, The End of Everything. Our interview is delayed because of wifi issues, which is fitting given that the novel is about – among many things – what happens when non-human intelligence takes over.

The End of Everything is the first sci-fi novel to have won the prize in its 58-year history, which is almost as long as Harrison has been writing. “It’s interesting,” he replies, when asked if he feels vindicated, “that something that has an SF-adjacent feel can be regarded as a serious book and given the Booker prize. My problem has always been that I don’t believe in genre. I don’t believe in it in any way.” He gently wags his finger at me. It is a bit like having coffee with a cheerier, more neatly bearded Gandalf – it will surprise no one that, in his youth, Harrison read The Lord of the Rings every year for a decade.

Whether he likes it or not, Harrison is hailed as a titan of literary science fiction. His fans have included giants such as the late Ursula K Le Guin and Iain Banks, as well as China Miéville today, and more surprisingly the Sex and the City star, and last year’s Booker judge, Sarah Jessica Parker. But he is not, as he would be the first to say, a household name. Although that has been changing. In 2020 he won the Goldsmiths prize for The Sunken Land Begins to Rise Again, and in 2022 he was himself a Booker judge.

The End of Everything took around 15 years to write, with real-world events overtaking him. AI, late capitalism, environmental collapse, the refugee crisis, Brexit – nearly all the manifestations of today’s omni-crisis can be found in the pages of this slim, elusive novel. As its title suggests, this is the work for our end times. “I suddenly thought, ‘Well, you’re 80, you might as well have a go at pushing it over the cliff one more time.’ My rule has always been push it as far as it will go, then move back slightly from the edge. But this time I thought, ‘Let’s push it over and see what happens.’”

And what happens is anyone’s guess. As critics have pointed out, The End of Everything deliberately resists definition. It is a triumph of obfuscation. “I could explain some of it to you,” the author says tantalisingly. “But no, I don’t want to.” For Harrison, the world ends not with a bang, but with endless confusion. “It was a book designed to present the explanatory collapse and epistemological collapse that you see in societies that have suddenly lost their grounding.”

He describes it as a mix of gothic horror, road movie, science fiction and fantasy – even “a seaside novel”. I would add satire to the list. One thing it is not, Harrison is clear, is a dystopia, but rather a post-disaster novel in the tradition of early JG Ballard or John Wyndham. But he wanted to play with the conventions; he didn’t want the reader to know more than the characters. “It would be ordinary sci-fi,” he says, “if you were told it was the triffids.”

Set in an unnamed coastal town somewhere in Kent (“If this is hell, it looks a lot like Margate,” as Peaky Blinders famously had it) in the nearish future, The End of Everything depicts a disintegrating Britain, after an invasion by an alien species called the iGhettis, which appear as “tall writhing bursts of light”. The iGhettis are a play on “I get it” (explanation), “I get stuff” (capitalism), Getty (extreme wealth), Apple (tech), I (Freud). “I wrote it down and I thought, ‘This is cheap.’ And then I looked at it again and thought, ‘Oh my God, there are so many ambiguities packed into that one word,’” he says with glee.

The germ of the novel was the financial crisis of 2007-8. “I had the rage, but I couldn’t make it work.” So he put what he had written away in a drawer and in 2015 “cannibalised” it for a short story called The Crisis. It was almost the end of him. During a reading of the story at an event in east London, he was struck by what felt like the worst indigestion of his life. “I thought, ‘That’ll teach you to down two glasses of red wine and eat pizza before performing.’” Two days later he was taken to hospital and told he’d had a heart attack. He was just shy of 70. When he returned to The Crisis, he realised it was the blueprint for a whole novel. “I was like, ‘Wow!’ And began to work on it.”

Harrison was born in Rugby, Warwickshire, in 1945. The closeness of the second world war overshadowed his childhood. “You were never allowed to forget it.” His father was an engineer, and the family lived on an estate of modern houses built for postwar key workers. One of the defining memories of his childhood was a Narnia-style wardrobe that, when he climbed into it, “was a library of trash novels” from 1920s thrillers to contemporary sci-fi magazines.

“It was full of all the things you weren’t supposed to enjoy,” he says with delight. He doesn’t know who the books belonged to. His parents had a very small bookcase with some classics downstairs in the lounge. “But it was the most extraordinary education for the imagination.” His father died when he was 13 and his mother never got over his death, something Harrison will explore if he ever writes his autobiography.

When he was 21, he published his first short story in the science-fiction magazine Science Fantasy. He became literary editor of New Worlds in 1968. He had a number of odd jobs – a groom at a hunting stables, a clerk, a trainee teacher. “Being a kind of hippy, I decided that if you were going to write, you would only write, and that you would take the consequences,” he says. That meant couch-surfing and often not having much to eat. “We were all living in appalling circumstances in west London before west London was west London,” he says of his fellow writers. “And it was great fun.”

Today he lives in rural Shropshire with his partner, the editor and writer Cath Phillips. He writes his first drafts in Moleskine notebooks, “always black and with squared paper” using Muji 0.5 pens, red and black. He is already working on an idea that may end up as a novel or short stories.

“Ever since I started in 1965,” he says, “my ambition has been to take down the divisions between genres. That’s been a guiding light.” As a reviewer for many years, he would ask: “Why should we be bad writers just because we’re writing science fiction? Why can’t we write good characters? Why shouldn’t we do it all?”

He is no longer angry with the publishing industry. “I’ve been mellowing as I age,” he says. He is now in his “late stage” as he calls it. “Older writers become knotty and gnarly. They just want to do what they want to do.” And this has worked. “I sold more books on the back of that position than I did by compromises with the industry.” And now he’s won its biggest prize.

The novel ends on what he calls “a positive” rather than a hopeful note. Does he feel hopeful for humanity? “No, I don’t feel any hope at all,” he replies bluntly. “We are just walking in a dream into a desperate situation. Somehow somebody has got to remind us that every action has consequences and that we’re ignoring them.”

Is that the responsibility of the novelist? “There are many,” he says. “To charm, to entertain. But I’ve always been Cassandra. It’s always a warning. ‘Be careful what you do.’”

  • The End of Everything by M. John Harrison (Profile, £16.99). To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.

entries.title: Killing the Pope review – the truth behind the attempted murder of John Paul II
entries.summary: Was the failed assassination of the Polish pope a Soviet plot or simply the work of a deranged hitman?On the afternoon of Wednesday 13 May 1981, St Peter’s Square in Rome was packed with more than 10,000 pilgrims, excited to see the charismatic John Paul II, formerly Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Kraków. On the afternoon of Wednesday 13 May 1981, St Peter’s Square in Rome was packed with more than 10,000 pilgrims, excited to see the charismatic John Paul II, formerly Karol Wojtyla, archbishop of Kraków. Two and a half years earlier he had become the youngest cardinal to be elected pope in more than a century and the first non-Italian for 455 years.

At 5.17pm a man pulled out a concealed pistol and raised it with both hands above the heads of the crowd. He took aim at the pope, only a few metres away, and fired several shots. Then, as he backed away from the shocked bystanders, he tripped and fell, where he lay pinned to the ground by a Franciscan nun until handcuffed by uniformed police. Meanwhile the pope had been hit by two bullets, one in the arm and the other in the abdomen. He was losing blood rapidly. He was rushed to hospital and underwent an operation, before beginning a slow recovery. The would-be assassin was soon revealed to be Mehmet Ali Ağca, a member of the rightwing Turkish paramilitary group known as the Grey Wolves.

Almost immediately speculation began that Ağca had not been acting alone. In his new book, Serhii Plokhy weighs the claim, first made in an Italian court, that the assassin had been “only the visible point of a conspiracy”. Plokhy has previously written several highly praised works, including Chernobyl: History of a Tragedy, which won the 2018 Baillie Gifford prize. He has a deserved reputation for careful research and reasoned evaluation.

Of several competing theories, the one that gained most traction was that Ağca was a tool of Bulgarian state security, acting on behalf of their Soviet masters. This is what the CIA came to believe, despite their initial scepticism. Plokhy himself admits that he set out feeling more sympathetic towards the proponents of the “Bulgarian connection” than to their opponents. There was a strong case to be made: the pope was in the frontline of the cold war. He was a Pole, Poland was overwhelmingly Catholic, and the church represented a challenge to communist rule.

In 1979, only nine months after being elected, John Paul II had made a visit to his homeland and had celebrated mass in the centre of Warsaw, in front of an audience of 300,000 Soon the Catholic church was providing financial and moral support to the new unofficial trade union, Solidarity, which was rapidly becoming a focus of civil resistance to the regime. In January 1981 Solidarity’s leader, Lech Wałęsa, had visited Rome and enjoyed a private audience with the pope. There was no doubt that the pressure for change in Poland caused deep concern in Moscow; the Russians threatened to invade if the Polish authorities didn’t suppress the uprising themselves.

And if the Russians doubted the power of a religious leader to cause political upheaval, they only had to look to Iran, where the return of Ayatollah Khomeini in 1979 had brought about the overthrow of a western-backed regime previously assumed to be stable. As for the Bulgarians, they had form: in 1978 they had employed an agent to assassinate Georgi Markov, a Bulgarian dissident in London, using a poisoned umbrella to stab him as he waited for a bus on Waterloo Bridge.

Hardline anti-communist embraced the theory uncritically. Yet one might equally well argue that, far from wanting him out of the way, the Soviet leadership needed the pope as a restraining influence on the Polish insurgency. An article in the official Russian newspaper Izvestiia argued instead that the Americans were responsible for the assassination through their funding neo-fascist and terrorist groups in Turkey.

Plokhy, for his part, has found no evidence of an international conspiracy, and changed his mind about “the Bulgarian connection”. In that sense the book is an anticlimax: there was no smoking gun, except the Browning dropped by Ağca in St Peter’s Square. Plokhy’s downbeat conclusion is that Ağca, like most assassins, was probably just another deranged individual seeking notoriety.

Ağca’s testimony during his interrogation and trial was contradictory and sometimes palpably false. To the neutral observer it was obvious that he was bargaining for a reduced sentence. Some of his claims were so fantastic as to lead the Italian magistrates to doubt his sanity. “I am Jesus Christ!” he shouted from his steel cage in the courtroom to reporters and cameramen gathered for the trial of his alleged Bulgarian accomplices, who were acquitted. Nevertheless people believed what they wanted to believe. The pope himself was convinced from the start that the KGB was behind the assassination attempt. In an act of extraordinary forgiveness, John Paul visited Ağca in prison and spent 20 minutes in private conversation with him.

John Paul II died in 2005. Ağca issued a statement from prison mourning the death of his “spiritual brother”, the man whom he had tried to kill. He was released in 2010. On 27 December 2014, 31 years to the day after the pope had visited him in prison, Ağca stood in front of John Paul’s tomb in the Vatican, and after a few moments of apparent silent meditation, laid some white roses there. For this stunt he was accompanied by a television crew.

Plokhy writes in clear, straight­forward prose. He has opted to use the present tense throughout and while this technique works well for the period immediately following the assassination, injecting an immediacy to the narrative, it is less effective and occasionally confusing when describing more recent events. Nevertheless, in telling this bizarre – at times even grotesque – story, he holds the reader’s attention to the end.
